classes.title: How a language model is built

questions.title: What it actually does
questions.q: You type a question and a paragraph comes back. What is the model doing?

options.A: Retrieving the closest matching answer from a knowledge database.
options.B: Predicting the next token, appending it, and running again on the longer text.
options.C: Understanding the question, then planning an answer, then writing it out.
options.D: Choosing between response templates learned during training.

questions.why: One operation, repeated. No separate understanding module, no knowledge database, no reasoning engine. Everything else in this course is built **around** that.

questions.title: Before it starts writing
questions.q: Before writing its first word, the model has already decided how the answer will end.
questions.why: Its own output is fed back in, one token at a time. It cannot plan its ending before it starts, and it never "knows" the answer in advance of writing it. Week 9 uses this to explain why chain-of-thought helps.

questions.title: The objective is not new
questions.q: Predicting the next word was already the standard task in NLP in the 1990s, using n-gram models. What is different about a transformer LLM?

options.A: The objective changed: n-grams predicted the next word, LLMs understand the sentence.
options.B: The objective is the same. What changed is the representation and how much context it can use.
options.C: n-gram models were hand-written rules; LLMs are statistical.
options.D: n-gram models predicted whole sentences at once; LLMs work word by word.

questions.why: Both predict what comes next — Shannon was doing it by hand in 1948. What changed is **how**: a count table with smoothing became learned vectors plus attention, and four words of context became a hundred thousand tokens. C. is the common misconception: n-grams were statistical too, just counting rather than learning.

questions.title: Letters
questions.q: Asked how many *p*'s are in **hippopotamus**, a model answers 2. Best explanation?

options.A: It cannot count reliably.
options.B: It never received the individual letters — it received **hip · pop · ot · amus**.
options.C: Its training data contained this mistake.
options.D: It needs fine-tuning on spelling tasks.

questions.why: A **perception** failure, not a reasoning one — the detail was destroyed before the model saw it. A. and D. assume the input was fine and the model was weak, and that misdiagnosis is what sends teams off to fine-tune something unfixable.

questions.title: Common and rare
questions.q: A tokenizer has a fixed vocabulary of roughly 200,000 chunks. Which of these becomes the **most** tokens?

options.A: `the`
options.B: `tokenization`
options.C: `hippopotamus`
options.D: They are all one token — that is what a vocabulary is for.

questions.why: `hip · pop · ot · amus`, 4 tokens. (`the` = 1, `tokenization` = `token · ization` = 2.) Common words earned their own entry in the list; rare ones did not, so they shatter into pieces. The tokenizer is not being clever: the list was built by merging the most frequent character pairs over and over, so a string common enough to have been merged all the way up survives whole, and anything else stops partway. This is also why an unusual name or a technical term costs you more than it looks.

questions.title: "Chinese costs more with LLMs"
questions.q: The same Chinese sentence became **29** tokens under a 100,000-entry vocabulary and **16** under a 200,000-entry one — the same as its English translation. What changed?

options.A: The newer model understands Chinese better.
options.B: The vocabulary was enlarged and the new entries were spent on Chinese words, so 自然 became one token instead of two.
options.C: Chinese text was compressed before being sent.
options.D: The newer model has a larger context window.

questions.why: Nothing about Chinese changed, and nothing about the model's intelligence. A **tokenizer is a design decision** made by the vendor, and it lands directly on your bill. The wider lesson: date your received wisdom — a lot of what people repeat about LLMs was measured on a model generation that no longer exists.

questions.title: Whose token?
questions.q: Two vendors quote you a price per 1,000 tokens, and both report that your document is "about 1,000 tokens". What do you need before those numbers can be compared?

options.A: The parameter count of each model.
options.B: Which tokenizer produced each count — every lab picks its own vocabulary.
options.C: The context window of each model.
options.D: Nothing: a token is a standard unit.

questions.why: A token count is only meaningful next to the name of the vocabulary that produced it. The same Chinese sentence is 29 tokens under `cl100k_base` and 16 under `o200k_base`, and Qwen, DeepSeek and Claude all ship their own. Claude's is not published, so you count those tokens through the API rather than locally.

questions.title: ID order
questions.q: Token IDs are assigned so that words with related meanings get nearby numbers.
questions.why: They are row numbers in a list, ordered by nothing relevant. *cat* is #4719 and *dog* is #18964 — and *kitten* is not even one row: it arrives as **#74 · #23257** (`k · itten`). Nothing in those numbers says a cat is more like a kitten than a dog.

questions.title: What built the vocabulary
questions.q: The algorithm that builds the vocabulary merges 自 and 然 into one token because it recognises 自然 as a word.
questions.why: It merged them because that pair is **frequent**. The merge algorithm is pure statistics on character frequency and knows nothing about meaning. Meaning does not come from the tokenizer.

questions.title: Where the table comes from
questions.q: The embedding table is learned during training, not written by hand.
questions.why: Nobody designs it. Tokens used in similar contexts get pushed towards similar numbers, as a side effect of being scored on predicting the next token. Meaning is a by-product of the prediction task.

questions.title: Not only position
questions.q: In a learned embedding space, the step from *France* to *Paris* turns out to be roughly the same step as from *Germany* to *Berlin*. What does that show?

options.A: The model has memorised a list of capital cities.
options.B: Meaning is carried by **direction** between vectors, not only by where a word sits.
options.C: The four words appear in the same sentences in the training data.
options.D: The embedding table was arranged alphabetically.

questions.why: Position carrying meaning is the intuitive half; the stronger claim is that the **step** between words carries meaning too, which is why you can do arithmetic on words: `Paris − France + Germany ≈ Berlin`. It is cleanest in the small dedicated embedding models of the 2010s and messier inside a modern LLM — a demonstration of the idea, not a party trick to reproduce live.

questions.title: What goes into the network
questions.q: The tokenizer has done its work and turned your sentence into tokens. What is actually fed into the neural network?

options.A: The text of each token, as characters.
options.B: The token IDs — the row numbers the tokenizer produced.
options.C: The embedding vectors those token IDs are used to look up.
options.D: A single vector representing the whole sentence.

questions.why: A token ID is only a row number, and there is no useful arithmetic to do on a row number: #4719 is not bigger than, or closer to, #18964 in any sense that means anything. The ID's one job is to pick a row out of the embedding table, and what the network receives is that row — a few thousand numbers, for each token. **Text → tokenizer → IDs → embedding table → vectors**, and everything the model does from there happens on the vectors.

questions.title: The same word twice
questions.q: In *"the bank by the river bank"*, both occurrences of *bank* come out of the embedding table with the same vector.
questions.why: Identical out of the table — and pulled apart immediately afterwards by their different neighbours. The table gives a **context-free** meaning; attention makes it **context-dependent**. After layer 1 there are two different vectors.

questions.title: One word changed
questions.q: *"The trophy didn't fit in the suitcase because **it** was too **big**"* → *it* = the trophy. *"…because **it** was too **small**"* → *it* = the suitcase. What does the flip demonstrate?

options.A: The model applies a grammar rule for resolving pronouns.
options.B: The grammar is identical in both sentences, so the referent must come from weighing which word is relevant given everything else present.
options.C: The model has memorised both sentences from training.
options.D: The model reads the sentence forwards, then backwards.

questions.why: A rule operating on structure alone must give the same answer twice, because the structure **is** the same. One adjective moved and the answer moved with it.

questions.title: A model that only pretrained
questions.q: A model that has finished pretraining only is asked *"What is the capital of France?"* and replies *"What is the capital of Germany? What is the capital of Italy?…"* What is happening?

options.A: It is refusing to answer.
options.B: It does not know the answer.
options.C: It is doing exactly its job — continuing a text that looks like a list of quiz questions.
options.D: The question was tokenized incorrectly.

questions.why: Pretraining produces something that **continues text**, not something that answers you. Paris is in there; the habit of answering is not. That gap is precisely what stages 2 and 3 close.

questions.title: What a worked example teaches
questions.q: A supervised fine-tuning set contains this pair, written by a person. Prompt: *"Customer message: my package arrived three days late and the box was crushed."* Response: *"I'm sorry — that's not the experience we want you to have. I've started a replacement and a refund; you'll get a confirmation email within the hour."* What does the model take away from this example?

options.A: That this particular customer's package arrived late.
options.B: A way of handling complaints: acknowledge it, fix it, name a concrete next step.
options.C: The company's refund and replacement policy.
options.D: That exact reply, to be repeated word for word the next time someone complains.

questions.why: Stage 2 teaches a **habit, not a fact**. The model comes away knowing nothing about this customer, nothing about company policy, and it is not memorising the sentence — it is learning the *shape* of a good answer, from tens of thousands of examples like this one. Which is also why the data decides the habit: had every response in the set been three defensive paragraphs of policy, you would have built a model that cannot be brief or helpful, and no prompt would fix it afterwards.

questions.title: Which stage?
questions.q: *"Our AI assistant must answer questions about the 2026 product catalogue, and the catalogue changes every few weeks."* What is the right way to deliver that?

options.A: Pretraining — knowledge comes from stage 1, so the catalogue has to go in there.
options.B: Supervised fine-tuning on the catalogue, repeated each time it changes.
options.C: Alignment — train it to prefer accurate answers about your products.
options.D: No training at all: put the relevant part of the catalogue into the context at question time.

questions.why: **B.** is the interesting wrong answer, because it is not impossible — facts *can* be pushed into a model by fine-tuning it on them. It is simply the expensive way to store something that is out of date next month, and you would pay for it again on every change. **A.** is out of reach: stage 1 finished long before you arrived, and you are not going to redo it. **C.** encodes preferences, and there is no preference here, only a fact. Supplying the catalogue at question time costs nothing to update, because you change the document rather than the model. Section B builds exactly this.

questions.title: Both answers are true
questions.q: A user says they are nervous about an interview. Answer **A** is warm and practical; answer **B** is an accurate textbook paragraph. Both are true. The model reliably produces **A**. Why?

options.A: Answer A is more factually accurate.
options.B: People were shown both and said which they preferred, and the model was trained on those judgements.
options.C: The model detects emotion and adjusts its tone.
options.D: Answer B exceeds the model's output limit.

questions.why: Stage 3 shows **pairs** and asks which is preferred — not which is correct. There is no fact to learn here, only a preference written down by an identifiable person. This is where tone, refusals and the model's whole personality come from, and why the same underlying model can feel like a different product in two places.

questions.title: Expensive is not the same as felt
questions.q: A model is built in three stages: **pretraining** (reads a huge amount of text), **supervised fine-tuning** (learns from example answers people wrote), **alignment** (learns from people's choices between two answers). Which pairing is right?

options.A: Most expensive: alignment. Most felt by the user: pretraining.
options.B: Most expensive: pretraining. Most felt by the user: alignment.
options.C: Most expensive: supervised fine-tuning. Most felt by the user: pretraining.
options.D: All three cost roughly the same and matter roughly equally.

questions.why: Stage 1 is months of compute on thousands of GPUs; stage 3 is a set of preference pairs, the cheapest of the three. Yet nearly everything a user reacts to — tone, warmth, refusals, whether the thing is pleasant to use — was decided in stage 3. Most of what people mean when they call a model "good" or "annoying" is the cheapest stage.

questions.title: Will you pretrain?
questions.q: Your board wants the company to train its own model from scratch. The strongest reason to say no:

options.A: It is illegal to train on internet data.
options.B: Frontier pretraining takes months on thousands of GPUs and is done by a few dozen organisations on earth — and you would still have stages 2 and 3 ahead of you.
options.C: Nobody knows how pretraining works.
options.D: A model you train yourself cannot be fine-tuned afterwards.

questions.why: Most people in this field build **on top of** frontier models, and that is a different and much larger job, not a lesser one. Note the shape of the question: what is examined is *why not pretrain*, and the reasoning earns the marks — never *how* to.

questions.title: The ring, not the box
questions.q: You join a company that is building a product on top of an existing LLM. What is most of the work?

options.A: Training and improving the model itself.
options.B: Writing prompts.
options.C: Choosing which model to buy, then maintaining the subscription.
options.D: Everything around the model — what you feed it, what it can reach, how you check it, what it is allowed to do.

questions.why: The model is a **component**, not a product. Almost nobody in this room will build the box; the job is the ring around it, and that ring is the rest of this course.

questions.title: Confidently wrong
questions.q: Asked about your company's leave policy, a general AI assistant replies that new joiners get 14 days, "accruing at 1.17 days per month". Your policy says 12 days, no accrual. What happened?

options.A: It was trained on another company's policy and confused the two.
options.B: It has never seen your documents, and produced the most plausible continuation — which is not the same as a true one.
options.C: Its training data is out of date; a newer model would know your policy.
options.D: It misread the question.

questions.why: The specificity is what makes it dangerous: a decimal reads as authority. C. is the tempting wrong answer — no model of any vintage has seen your internal documents, so no upgrade fixes it.

questions.title: What a prompt can change
questions.q: Your AI assistant has never seen your company's leave policy. Adding *"only answer if you are certain, and do not guess"* to the prompt will make it able to answer leave questions correctly.
questions.why: That instruction is worth adding, and it does something real: the model becomes more likely to say "I don't know" instead of inventing a number, and silence beats a confident wrong answer. But saying nothing is not the same as answering, and the policy is still not in there — no wording can put it there. **Prompting changes behaviour, never knowledge.** That sentence is the whole reason RAG exists.

questions.title: Making the output usable
questions.q: You ask a model for the name and the days in each leave request, and your code saves them to a database. Three replies come back:
questions.example:
Chan Tai Man is asking for 5 days.
The request is from Wong Siu Ming, and it is for 3 days of leave.
Name: Lee Ka Yan / Days: 10
questions.q_after: Your code cannot read them. Cheapest fix?

options.A: Add the output shape to the prompt: *reply with only `{"name": "...", "days": 0}` and nothing else.*
options.B: Write code that handles every sentence shape the model might produce.
options.C: Fine-tune the model on correctly formatted answers.
options.D: Send the first model's answer to a second model and ask it to reformat.

questions.why: Free, instant, undone in one line. Nobody told the model what shape you needed, so it picked one — a new one each time. B. is a losing race: there is always a fourth shape. C. and D. spend real money on what a sentence fixes. Fixed output shape, examples in the prompt (*few-shot*), work step by step (*chain of thought*) — that is what "prompting is engineering" means.

questions.title: Why RAG exists
questions.q: In one line, what does RAG do?

options.A: Finds the few passages that might contain the answer, pastes them into the prompt, and asks the question with them attached.
options.B: Trains the model on your documents overnight, so it wakes up knowing them.
options.C: Lets the model browse your file server while it is answering.
options.D: Compresses your documents so they fit in the context window.

questions.why: Retrieve first, then answer. It exists because the model does not know your organisation's documents and never will. Everything else about RAG is engineering.

questions.title: It had the passage and still got it wrong
questions.q: Your AI assistant uses RAG and gives a wrong answer. You print out everything that was sent to the model. The correct passage is there in full, and nothing else that was sent contradicts that passage. The answer contradicts it anyway. Which stage do you fix?

options.A: Retrieval — the search returned the wrong thing.
options.B: The embedding model — the question and the passage are worded too differently to match.
options.C: Chunking — the passage was split badly.
options.D: Generation — the evidence was there and was not used.

questions.why: Right passage, wrong answer = generation. The other three are ruled out by the prompt in front of you: the passage arrived, so retrieval worked (A.) and the embeddings matched (B.); it arrived whole, so chunking was fine (C.). Every fix attaches to a stage, so naming the stage is the skill — and the prompt that was actually sent is where you look.

questions.title: The chunk that lost its heading
questions.q: In a RAG system, a chunk that cuts a table in half can still look perfectly relevant to the search, while no longer saying what its numbers refer to.
questions.why: `Grade 7+ ....... 25 days` retrieved without the heading above it scores well and reads fine — but nothing in it says *which* leave. This is the failure nobody predicts, and internal documents are mostly tables and forms. The standard fix is repeating the heading into every chunk.

questions.title: Twenty-five million against ten trillion
questions.q: You want an AI assistant that answers questions about your company's 3,000 internal PDFs. Your team proposes training a general model further on those PDFs as raw text — the documents as they are, no question-and-answer pairs written. Why will that not work?

options.A: Raw text cannot be used for training; only prompt-and-response pairs can.
options.B: Continued pretraining only works on publicly available text.
options.C: Your 3,000 PDFs come to a few tens of millions of tokens, against the trillions the model has already read. One pass over them changes almost nothing — and enough passes to force the facts in damages what the model knew before.
options.D: The model would refuse to answer questions about private documents.

questions.why: **Continued pretraining** on raw text is a real technique — it is how domain-specialised models are built — so the objection is scale, not legality or format. Three thousand PDFs is roughly one part in four hundred thousand of what the base model has read. Forcing the facts in means many repetitions, and that is **catastrophic forgetting**. A. is wrong for an instructive reason: raw text is exactly what continued pretraining takes. It is **SFT** that needs pairs.

questions.title: Facts in the weights
questions.q: Your AI assistant can hold the policy two ways: trained into the model, or left in your documents and looked up when someone asks. Both answer correctly. What does the trained-in version lose?

options.A: The answer arrives with no source, it is stale from the moment the policy is amended, and it cannot be withheld from a reader who should not have seen that document.
options.B: It would be too slow to answer.
options.C: Its answers would come out in the wrong format.
options.D: None — a model that has memorised the policy is the better system.

questions.why: Three losses at once: no source, no way to update short of training again, and no per-person permissions — a document inside the weights is readable by anyone who can reach the model. Retrieval checks permissions when the question is asked, and hands back the file and page it used.

questions.title: What fine-tuning actually trains on
questions.q: You have decided to fine-tune a model so that it answers in your company's house style. What does supervised fine-tuning (SFT) take as its training data?

options.A: Your company's internal documents, as raw text.
options.B: A list of facts, one per line.
options.C: The model's own previous answers, fed back unedited.
options.D: Prompt-and-response pairs that you write: a question, and the answer you wanted.

questions.why: Almost every time someone says "fine-tuning" they mean SFT, and its unit is the **pair**. A. describes continued pretraining, a different technique with a different problem. The quantity surprises people in the other direction: a few hundred to a few thousand pairs is a normal set for teaching a house voice — not millions. Turning three thousand documents into pairs is a project of its own, which is part of why this is the wrong tool for facts.

questions.title: When prompting will not hold
questions.q: Your AI assistant answers correctly but never in your company's house style, and no amount of prompt rewriting has fixed it. What now?

options.A: Retrieval — give it documents written in the house style.
options.B: Add "use our house style" to the system prompt again, more firmly.
options.C: Change to a bigger model.
options.D: Fine-tune it on examples written in the house style.

questions.why: Style, format and vocabulary are exactly what fine-tuning is **for** — once prompting has genuinely been tried and failed to hold. A. is the common wrong turn: retrieval changes what the model can *see*, not the manner in which it writes. These are three **strategies** for three different faults, not steps you climb; you pick the one that matches the fault, and where two would fit, the cheaper.

questions.title: What fine-tuning is for
questions.q: Fine-tuning is the reliable way to teach a model your company's facts.
questions.why: RAG changes **what the model knows**; fine-tuning changes **how it behaves**. Fine-tuning on your facts can memorise the specific answers you wrote down, which is not the same as knowing the policy: it will not generalise to the questions you did not write, it cannot be updated without another training run, and it cannot cite the document the answer came from.

questions.title: Not an escalation
questions.q: If RAG cannot answer a question, fine-tuning is the next thing to try.
questions.why: Prompting, retrieval and fine-tuning are three **strategies** for three different faults, not three stages of one thing. If retrieval could not find the information, the information is still missing after a training run — a more expensive method is not a stronger version of a cheaper one. A failed attempt almost always means the fault was diagnosed wrongly: the grade 7 answer was lost to **chunking**, and what fixed it was chunking.

questions.title: What an agent is
questions.q: An agent is:

options.A: A model that has been fine-tuned to be more autonomous.
options.B: Several models talking to each other.
options.C: A model that can use tools to act, read what comes back, and keep going until the job is done.
options.D: A model with a much larger context window.

questions.why: A **tool** is a function the model can call, described to it in words — `get_leave_balance(staff_id)`. Some tools come with the assistant you are using; others you add yourself. Either way the model decides when to call one and with what, reads the result, and decides again. Think → call → read → repeat, until done. That loop is what separates an agent from a model that only answers.

questions.title: The loop wrote something
questions.q: A user asks an agent to file leave for Monday but never gives a staff number, and none is on file. The agent calls `submit_leave("E0001", "2026-09-07")`, gets a confirmation, and replies "Booked." What happened, and why does it matter more than a wrong answer in chat?

options.A: It picked the wrong tool; nothing was written, so the cost is an apology.
options.B: It invented an argument — and because the tool **writes**, leave is now filed against someone else's record and nothing raised an error.
options.C: It ran out of context and lost the staff number.
options.D: It never stopped, and retried until a call succeeded.

questions.why: The moment a tool writes to a real system, failures stop being embarrassing and start being expensive. A wrong sentence is embarrassing; a wrong `submit_leave` call is an HR incident — and it looked like a success from every angle.

questions.title: Worth thinking about?
questions.q: A reasoning model spends more compute before answering — slower and dearer. Which request justifies it?

options.A: "What is our office address?"
options.B: "Summarise this support ticket in one sentence."
options.C: "Given our leave policy, the public holiday calendar and this employee's start date, how much leave can they take before December?"
options.D: "Translate this paragraph into Cantonese."

questions.why: The win only shows up on genuinely **multi-step** problems, where each step depends on the last. On a single lookup you have paid for thinking and received the same answer, slower — and latency is a cost the user feels but the invoice never shows.

questions.title: Where the bill goes
questions.q: An employee's leave question, with your instructions around it, is 200 tokens. Retrieval adds 4,000 tokens of HR policy. Both go to the model in one prompt, and you pay for every token in it. What do the 4,000 against the 200 tell you?

options.A: Almost every token you send is passage text that retrieval put there, not the employee's own words.
options.B: The employee's question is the main thing driving your cost.
options.C: Retrieval is free, because it runs before the model does.
options.D: In every system, what the model writes back costs more than what you send it.

questions.why: RAG made the bill bigger: retrieved passages are tokens too, paid for again on **every question**. C. gets the order right and the money wrong — the search is cheap, but its result goes to the model, and that is what you pay for. This is not an argument against RAG. It is why chunk size and how many passages you retrieve are **cost** decisions, not only quality ones.

questions.title: The document that gives orders
questions.q: Your AI assistant reads every file on a shared drive. Someone puts a file there with instructions hidden inside it. Your assistant can end up following those instructions.
questions.why: **Indirect prompt injection.** Hidden text in the file — white text on page 6, say, telling the assistant to email the staff list outside — is retrieved with the real content and lands in the prompt, and the model cannot tell "text to read" from "orders to follow". The attacker never opened your assistant and never held an account, so there is nobody to ban. If the assistant can send email, the hidden line does not spoil an answer — it acts.

questions.title: What can come back out
questions.q: Anything placed in the model's context — retrieved passages, system instructions, another user's document — can come back out in an answer.
questions.why: The third failure: it leaks. Note that all three — fabricates, obeys its input, leaks — got **worse** the moment you added retrieval and tools. Every capability added in Section B widened the attack surface.

questions.title: Where guardrails live
questions.q: You can add one protection before Monday to an agent that reads uploaded documents and can send email. Which, and why that one?

options.A: Instruct the model in the system prompt never to follow instructions found in documents.
options.B: Require human confirmation before anything irreversible — here, before any outbound email.
options.C: Switch to a model with stronger safety training.
options.D: Ask users to report suspicious answers.

questions.why: The model cannot be trusted to police itself, so guardrails live **around** it: input filtering, output validation, tool allow-lists, and a human before anything irreversible. B. is the only option that fails safe when everything else has already gone wrong, and it does not depend on detecting the attack.

questions.title: Two pieces, not one
questions.q: GPT-4o's tokenizer turns **tokenization** into two pieces, **token** and **ization**, but leaves **the** as one piece. Why?

options.A: Longer words are always split into two.
options.B: The tokenizer merged the strings that were common in its training text; **the** was common enough to survive whole, **tokenization** was not.
options.C: The model splits any word it does not understand.
options.D: Splitting keeps every piece roughly the same number of letters.

questions.why: Merges are learned by counting pairs in a training text. Frequency decides what stays whole — not length, not meaning, and nothing about the model that comes later.

questions.title: Frozen before training starts
questions.q: A model that keeps meeting a new word can add it to its tokenizer's vocabulary as it goes.
questions.why: The vocabulary is built once, from a training text, before the model is trained, and is then frozen for life. A new piece would have no row in the embedding table and no score at the output, both of which are sized in advance.

questions.title: How many numbers is a table of vectors
questions.q: GPT-2 has a vocabulary of 50,257 pieces and gives each one a vector of 768 numbers. How many numbers does its embedding matrix hold?
questions.why: The matrix is V × d, so multiply: 50,257 × 768 = 38,597,376, about 38.6 million. **C.** adds the two instead. **A.** is one row and **B.** is one number per piece — both forget that every piece gets a whole vector.

questions.title: Two vectors, one number
questions.q: Two toy vectors: **queen** = [0.6, 0.8] and **pizza** = [−0.6, 0.8]. What is their dot product?
questions.why: Multiply matching positions and add: 0.6 × (−0.6) = −0.36, 0.8 × 0.8 = 0.64, and −0.36 + 0.64 = 0.28. **C.** drops the minus sign, **A.** stops after the first pair, and **D.** is king · queen from the same slide.

questions.title: Nobody wrote it down
questions.source: 3:3 (a word is represented by its context)
questions.q: In the five-sentence table where **cat** and **dog** both appear with *drinks* and *eats*, their similarity had to be entered by hand.
questions.why: It falls out of counting which words they appear with. Nobody recorded that cats and dogs are alike — cat · dog = 2 and cat · car = 0 came from the counts alone. That is the whole idea the rest of the lecture builds on.

questions.title: Nearly all zero
questions.q: Counting contexts on real text gives **cat** one column per vocabulary word: 200,019 numbers, nearly all of them zero. What does word2vec do instead?

options.A: It counts the same table, then throws away the rare columns.
options.B: It fixes the width in advance — say 300 numbers — and learns them by predicting the neighbours.
options.C: It counts only the words that appear more than a hundred times.
options.D: It stores the table more efficiently on disk.

questions.why: The problem is not storage, it is that almost every number carries no information. Fixing d in advance and learning the values gives 300 numbers that all do work.

questions.title: Why divide by the total
questions.source: 4:2 (turning a dot product into a probability)
questions.q: In word2vec, c is the centre word and o an outside word in its window: P(o ∣ c) = exp(uo⊤ vc)  / ∑w ∈ V exp(uw⊤ vc). What does dividing by that sum achieve?

options.A: It makes every number positive.
options.B: It makes the numbers add up to 1, so they can be read as probabilities.
options.C: It makes rare words more likely.
options.D: It removes dot products that came out negative.

questions.why: Exponentiating is what makes each score positive — that job is done before the division. Dividing by the total over the whole vocabulary is what turns a pile of positive numbers into a distribution that adds up to 1.

questions.title: Read one probability off a softmax
questions.q: Five words are scored. After exponentiating, the values are 7.39, 2.72, 1.22, 0.61 and 0.22, adding up to 12.16. What probability does softmax give the **second** word?
questions.why: Divide by the total: 2.72 ÷ 12.16 = 0.22. **D.** skips the dividing step, **B.** divides by the number of words instead of by the total, and **C.** is the first word's share — 7.39 ÷ 12.16.

questions.title: The size of the step
questions.q: Training repeats one line: θnew = θold − α ∂J/∂θ. What does α control?

options.A: How wrong the model currently is.
options.B: How much of the gradient each step applies.
options.C: Which direction is downhill.
options.D: How many word vectors the model has.

questions.why: The derivative gives the direction *and* the steepness; the minus sign turns it downhill. α scales it, so the distance moved is α times the gradient rather than a fixed length — steep places move further. Too small and training crawls; too big and it steps over the bottom.

questions.title: The same row either way
questions.source: 6:1 (one row per word is not enough)
questions.q: After word2vec training, **bank** in *I sat on the river bank* and **bank** in *I withdrew money from the bank* have different vectors.
questions.why: The look-up is by token, so both sentences reach the same id and the same row of E. One row per word, whatever the sentence says — and no amount of extra training changes that, because the word has two meanings and the table has one row.

questions.title: The model cannot read
questions.q: A language model is given the letters of your sentence and works out what they mean.
questions.why: It does arithmetic on numbers and nothing else. The letters are turned into pieces, the pieces into ids, and the ids into vectors before the model sees anything — which is what the whole of this section is about.

questions.title: Why not one number per word
questions.q: A tokenizer could give one number to each whole English word. Why is that not what anyone does?

options.A: New words never stop arriving — names, typos, `COMP5423`, 香港 — and a fixed word list cannot cover them.
options.B: Sentences would become far too long to process.
options.C: English does not have enough words to fill a vocabulary.
options.D: Words carry no meaning until they are split up.

questions.why: A word list is finite and language is not. **B.** is the problem with the opposite design — one number per letter — where "cat" becomes three meaningless pieces and sentences get very long. Tokens are the compromise between the two.

questions.title: How a merge is chosen
questions.q: A tokenizer is being trained on a text. How is each new merge chosen?

options.A: The pair of neighbouring pieces that appears most often is joined into one piece.
options.B: The longest word in the text is added to the vocabulary.
options.C: Pairs are joined in alphabetical order.
options.D: A linguist marks which pieces carry meaning.

questions.why: Count every adjacent pair, join the commonest, and repeat. Nothing in the procedure knows what a word means — which is why the merges a tokenizer learns depend entirely on the text it was trained on.

questions.title: A word the tokenizer has never seen
questions.q: Training is over and the merge list is frozen. What does the tokenizer do with a word it has never seen before?

options.A: Applies the merges it already learned, in order, until no more of them fit.
options.B: Adds the word to its vocabulary and gives it a new id.
options.C: Splits it into single letters and leaves them.
options.D: Returns an error, so the word must be removed first.

questions.why: Encoding just runs the same merge list on new text. Any word, however unusual, comes out as pieces the tokenizer already has — so nothing is ever rejected, and nothing is ever added to the vocabulary.

questions.title: What the id is for
questions.q: In a language model, a token's id is the number the layers do their arithmetic on.
questions.why: The id is an address, not a value. It selects one row of E, and that row — 768 numbers for GPT-2 — is what everything downstream works with. Id 10,346 is not "bigger" than id 500 in any sense the model uses.

questions.title: A dot product of zero
questions.q: With toy vectors, king · queen comes to 0.96 and king · pizza comes to 0.00. What does the second number say?

options.A: The two vectors point in unrelated directions — nothing shared.
options.B: *pizza* is the opposite of *king*.
options.C: *pizza* is a rare word in the training text.
options.D: One of the two vectors has not been trained yet.

questions.why: A dot product is large when two vectors point the same way, and zero when they share nothing. **B.** would show up as a *negative* number, not zero — opposite and unrelated are different things.

questions.title: What word2vec is asked to predict
questions.q: word2vec slides a window along the text, taking the word in the middle as the centre word. At each position, what is word2vec trained to do?

options.A: Make the words around the centre word more likely.
options.B: Make the word that comes next more likely.
options.C: Decide whether two words are synonyms.
options.D: Decide which sentence the centre word came from.

questions.why: Skip-gram predicts the *neighbours* on both sides, not what follows. **B.** is the task of the next section — a language model — and swapping one for the other is the whole difference between the two halves of this week.

questions.title: What makes the loss small
questions.q: word2vec's loss J is a single number that training tries to make small. When is J small?

options.A: When the words that really were neighbours got high probability.
options.B: When every word in the vocabulary got the same probability.
options.C: When the word vectors all end up the same length.
options.D: When the vocabulary has been made as small as possible.

questions.why: J is the average log probability the model gave the true neighbours, with a minus sign in front. Predict them well and J falls. That one number is the whole definition of "good" the training has.

questions.title: One step downhill
questions.q: A model is being trained by gradient descent. One of its numbers stands at 0.80, the gradient ∂J/∂θ there is 2.0, and the learning rate α is 0.1. What is that number after one step?
questions.why: θnew = 0.80 − 0.1 × 2.0 = 0.60. **D.** adds where the minus sign says subtract, **A.** forgets α and takes the whole gradient as the step, and **B.** is the size of the step rather than the number it lands on.

questions.title: Similarity, straight off the table
questions.source: 3:3 (a word is represented by its context)
questions.q: Each row counts how often that word appeared with each context word:
questions.example:
drinks   eats   needs
   cat          1       1       0
   dog          1       1       0
   car          0       0       1
questions.q_after: Taking the rows as vectors, what is **cat** · **car**?
questions.why: Multiply the entries in matching positions and add: 1×0 + 1×0 + 0×1 = 0. Nothing is shared, so the score is zero. The same arithmetic on **cat** and **dog** gives 1 + 1 + 0 = 2 — which is how counting alone shows that cats and dogs are alike.

questions.title: Two merges and stop
questions.q: BPE joins the commonest neighbouring pair into one new piece, then repeats. Train it on this text, starting from the single characters and stopping when the vocabulary holds 5 pieces:
questions.example: a b a b a b c

options.A: a, b, c, ab, abab
options.B: a, b, c, ab, ba
options.C: a, b, c, ab, aba
options.D: ab, abab, c

questions.why: Two merges fit. `ab` appears three times, more than any other pair, so it is added as id 3. The text is now `ab ab ab c`, where `ab`+`ab` appears twice and becomes id 4. **C.** joins `ab` to a single `a` instead. **D.** drops the characters, which stay in the vocabulary for ever.

questions.title: Encode with a frozen vocabulary
questions.q: Training is over and the vocabulary is frozen. To encode, join the neighbouring pair with the smallest id, and repeat until no pair is in the vocabulary.

options.B: `a` · `aaab`

questions.why: `aa` has the smallest id, so it is joined first, at the leftmost place it fits: `aa a a b`. `aa` wins again: `aa aa b`. Now `aaaa` and `aab` are not in the vocabulary, so it stops — ids 4, 4, 1. **B.** reaches for the longest piece, but those letters were used two merges earlier.

questions.title: The run that stops early
questions.q: BPE joins the commonest neighbouring pair into one new piece, then repeats. It stops when the vocabulary is full, or earlier if no pair appears twice. There is room for 8 pieces:

options.A: a, b, c, d, ab
options.B: a, b, c, d, ab, abc, cab, abd
options.C: a, b, c, d, ab, abab
options.D: a, b, c, d

questions.why: `ab` is the only pair that appears twice, so it is joined: the text becomes `ab c ab d`. Every pair left — `ab`+`c`, `c`+`ab`, `ab`+`d` — appears once, so training stops with three slots unused. **B.** fills the vocabulary anyway. **C.** merges the two `ab`s, which are not neighbours.

questions.title: A letter that joins nothing
questions.q: Training is over and the vocabulary is frozen. To encode, join the neighbouring pair with the smallest id, and repeat until no pair is in the vocabulary.

options.B: `d` · `aab`
options.D: `da` · `ab`

questions.why: `da` is not in the vocabulary, so `d` joins nothing. `aa` is, and it has the smallest id, so it goes first: `d aa b`. Now `daa` and `aab` are not there either, so it stops. **B.** glues `aa` and `b` into a piece that was never learned. **C.** takes `ab`, id 5, over `aa`, id 4.

questions.title: What the model outputs
questions.q: Given the text so far, what does a language model output?

options.A: The single word it judges most likely to come next.
options.B: A probability for every token in the vocabulary, none negative and adding up to 1.
options.C: A short ranked list of the few most likely next words.
options.D: One number saying how likely the text so far is.

questions.why: The model never picks a word. It reports how likely each of the 200,019 tokens is, and something outside it — greedy choice, sampling, top-p — turns that into the one word you see. **A.** and **C.** describe that later step, not the model.

questions.title: Predicting and scoring
questions.q: A language model gives you the probability of each next token. Why does that also let you score a whole sentence?

options.A: Because the chain rule lets you multiply the probability of each word given the words before it.
options.B: Because sentence probabilities are stored separately during training.
options.C: Because the model averages the probabilities of the words in the sentence.
options.D: Because a sentence is scored by its longest word.

questions.why: P(w1 … wT) is the product of P(wt ∣ w1 … wt-1) over the whole sentence. No approximation is involved — it is conditional probability written out — so a next-word predictor is a sentence scorer for free.

questions.title: Only the last word
questions.q: A bigram model replaces P(wt ∣ w1 … wt-1) with P(wt ∣ wt-1). What is the honest description of that move?

options.A: An exact rewriting that loses nothing.
options.B: An assumption that is plainly false, made because it is what allows the probabilities to be counted.
options.C: A way of saving computer memory with no effect on the model's answers.
options.D: A rule that only applies to sentences shorter than ten words.

questions.why: The subject of a long sentence often decides its final verb, so one word of history is not enough. The trade is deliberate: conditioning on the whole history would need a probability for every possible history, and there are infinitely many.

questions.title: Score a sentence by hand
questions.source: 3:3 (a bigram model on a three-sentence corpus)
questions.q: Train a bigram model by counting on this corpus:
questions.example:
the cat sat
the cat ran
the dog sat
questions.q_after: Every sentence starts with **the**. What probability does the model give **the dog sat**?
questions.why: P(the) = 1; **the** is followed by **dog** once in three; **dog** is followed by **sat** every time. So 1 × 1/3 × 1 = 0.33. **A.** and **B.** give **dog** a split it does not have — it is followed by **sat** and nothing else.

questions.title: How many pairs are there
questions.q: A bigram model needs one number for every ordered pair of words. With a vocabulary of 1,000 words, how many pairs is that?
questions.why: Every word can follow every word: 1,0002=1,000,000. **C.** halves it, forgetting that order matters — *dog ran* and *ran dog* are different pairs. **D.** is the count for triples. A real vocabulary of 50,000 gives 2.5 billion pairs.

questions.title: One missing pair
questions.q: A bigram model scores a grammatical English sentence at exactly 0. What happened?

options.A: Every word in it was missing from the training text.
options.B: One pair of neighbouring words never appeared in the training text, and a single zero makes the whole product zero.
options.C: The sentence was longer than the model's window.
options.D: The probabilities were too small and were rounded down.

questions.why: The sentence's score is a product of pair probabilities. One unseen pair contributes 0, and zero times anything is zero — so the model rates a perfectly ordinary sentence exactly as likely as nonsense.

questions.title: What add-one cannot do
questions.q: After add-one smoothing, a bigram model that has seen **delicious pizza** many times gives **tasty pizza** a higher probability than **pizza the of**.
questions.why: Add-one spreads the same small amount over every unseen pair, so both come out identical. It has no way to notice that *tasty* and *delicious* are alike, because it treats every word as a separate symbol.

questions.title: No place to record that two words are alike
questions.q: A counting model has seen **delicious pizza** many times and **tasty pizza** never. Why does it have no way to know that *tasty* and *delicious* mean something similar?

options.A: It has not been given enough text yet.
options.B: It stores one count per word pair, so every word is a separate symbol with nothing linking it to any other.
options.C: Smoothing has already made the two pairs equally likely.
options.D: The two words are split into different tokens.

questions.why: Counting works on strings, and *tasty* and *delicious* are different strings. The table has no slot that says two words behave alike, so there is nothing for the model to consult. More text adds counts; it never adds that slot.

questions.title: Table or function
questions.q: An n-gram model and a neural language model both give a probability for the next token. How do the two get that number?

options.A: The n-gram model reads it from a table of counts; the neural model computes it with a function whose weights are used for every input.
options.B: The n-gram model predicts one word at a time; the neural model predicts the whole sentence at once.
options.C: The n-gram model produces raw counts; only the neural model produces probabilities.
options.D: The n-gram model works on whole words; the neural model works on single letters.

questions.why: Same task, two machines. The table holds one independent number per pair, so nothing learned in one entry reaches another. The function reuses its weights on every input, which is what lets two similar inputs come out with similar answers.

questions.title: Where the vectors come from
questions.q: In a modern language model, the embedding matrix is trained first on its own and then held fixed while the rest of the model is trained.
questions.why: The embedding matrix sits inside θ with everything else, and one gradient trains all of it together. The vectors are not prepared in advance to be generally useful — they are shaped by whatever makes next-word prediction good.

questions.title: Which fraction
questions.q: A bigram model estimates P(wt ∣ wt-1) by counting. Which fraction does it use?

options.A: count of the pair, divided by the count of the **first** word.
options.B: count of the pair, divided by the count of the **second** word.
options.C: count of the pair, divided by the total number of pairs in the text.
options.D: count of the second word, divided by the total number of words.

questions.why: You are asking "given that the first word appeared, how often did this one follow?", so the bottom counts every time the first word appeared. That is the whole training procedure: count pairs, divide, done.

questions.title: Which word follows cat
questions.source: 3:3 (a bigram model on a three-sentence corpus)
questions.q: Count the pairs in this corpus:
questions.example:
the cat sat
the cat ran
the dog sat
questions.q_after: What probability does the bigram model give P(sat ∣ cat)?
questions.why: **cat** appears twice, followed once by **sat** and once by **ran**, so each gets 1/2. Compare **dog**, which appears once and is followed by **sat** every time, giving 1.

questions.title: Making it write
questions.source: 3:4 (generation by sampling from a bigram model)
questions.q: You have a bigram model built by counting. What has to be added before it can write text of its own?

options.A: Nothing. Start from a word, draw the next one from its probabilities, append it, and repeat.
options.B: A second model, trained to generate rather than to score.
options.C: A grammar that checks each sentence before it is produced.
options.D: A list of sentence templates collected from the training text.

questions.why: Scoring and generating are the same machine pointed in different directions. That is true of every model in this course: the thing that says how likely a word is, is also the thing that writes.

questions.title: Probabilities, not scores
questions.q: Some of the numbers a language model gives for the next token can be negative, if a word is very unlikely.
questions.why: They are probabilities: never below zero, and adding up to exactly 1 across the whole vocabulary. A very unlikely word gets a tiny positive number — 0.0000001, not −0.3.

questions.title: Which transcription
questions.q: A speech recogniser hears one sound and cannot tell whether it was "recognise speech" or "wreck a nice beach". How does a language model settle it?

options.A: It gives each sentence a probability, and the likelier one is kept.
options.B: It looks both up in a dictionary of valid English sentences.
options.C: It prefers whichever sentence has fewer words.
options.D: It listens to the sound again and writes its own transcription.

questions.why: The two sound identical, so the audio cannot decide. Scoring a whole sentence is exactly what the chain rule buys you: roughly 2.1×10-5 against 8×10-10, so the first wins easily. Ranking candidates like this is what language models did for decades before they generated anything.

questions.title: What a trigram model costs
questions.q: A trigram model looks back two words instead of one. What does that buy, and what does it cost?

options.A: More of the history is used, but there are vastly more sequences to count and almost all of them are never seen.
options.B: More of the history is used, at no cost — a trigram model is simply better.
options.C: Less memory is needed, because longer sequences are rarer.
options.D: The model can no longer be built by counting at all.

questions.why: With 50,000 words there are 2.5 billion pairs but 125 trillion triples. Each step back uses more context and makes the counts sparser, and that trade is why n-gram models stopped at three or four.

questions.title: Counting every three-word sequence
questions.q: A trigram model needs one count for every three-word sequence. With a 50,000-word vocabulary that is 125 trillion counts, so most of them stay zero however much text you train on.
questions.why: 50,0003 = 125 trillion — more three-word sequences than there are words in everything ever written down. A triple is missing not because it is bad English but because no amount of text could ever contain them all.

questions.title: What add-one actually does
questions.q: Add-one smoothing is applied to a bigram model. What happens to a pair that was never seen?

options.A: It gets a small probability, so sentences containing it are no longer impossible.
options.B: It gets the probability of the most similar pair that *was* seen.
options.C: It gets the average probability of all the pairs that were seen.
options.D: Nothing — smoothing only adjusts pairs that already have counts.

questions.why: One is added to every count, so an unseen pair goes from 0 to 1 over a large bottom — tiny, but not zero. **B.** is what we would like it to do and exactly what it cannot: it has no notion that two pairs are similar.

questions.title: What end to end means
questions.q: A modern language model is described as trained *end to end*. What does that mean?

options.A: Token ids go in and probabilities come out, and every number in between is learned by the same procedure.
options.B: It is shown the training text in order, from the first document to the last.
options.C: Each layer is trained on its own and the trained layers are joined afterwards.
options.D: Training continues until the loss reaches zero.

questions.why: Once the text has been tokenized, there is no preparation step and no handover: the embedding sits in the parameters next to everything else, and one gradient moves all of it at once. The tokenizer itself is not part of this — its vocabulary is frozen before training.

questions.title: Smoothing, by hand
questions.q: A bigram model is trained on this corpus, whose vocabulary is its five words:
questions.example:
the cat sat
the cat ran
the dog sat
questions.q_after: With add-one smoothing, what is P(cat ∣ the)?
questions.why: Add 1 on top and V = 5 underneath: (2 + 1) / (3 + 5) = 3/8. **C.** is the unsmoothed 2/3, **D.** adds 1 to both top and bottom, and **A.** adds V underneath but forgets the 1 on top.
